newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian rain buoys crop, sinks prices - Grainco.
newsitem.headline: Australian rain buoys crop, sinks prices - Grainco.

text.p: Rain over the past week in southern Queensland, New South Wales (NSW) and South Australia (SA) was welcome for winter crop planting but had also depressed domestic sorghum values, Queensland grain cooperative Grainco Ltd said in its weekly market report.
Early week sorghum consumer buying interest in Brisbane, Newcastle, Sydney and Melbourne became subdued or eased to lower levels later in the week, trading manager Rob Brealey said.
Rain was mostly patchy and would not result in wholesale planting of winter cereals at present but the market was feeling a little more comfortable and in the short-term stood back.

By the end of last week, southern Queensland sorghum had eased to just under A$150.00 a tonne Brisbane for May. Central Queensland values received support from the prospect of sales to southern domestic markets and finished at about A$130.00 port.
New crop feed barley values eased on a lack of good news.
Rain brought the start of winter cereal planting in southern Queensland and parts of the southern states.
While the export market was currently subdued, domestic issues could support longer-term values, he said.
Most of Australia's barley producing areas had received some rain and begun planting but all required further general rainfall for additional planting, Brealey said.
Potential support from wheat prices, if a problem emerged in major producing or exporting countries, could not be ruled out.
Recent rainfall in southern Queensland has had little impact on short-term old crop feed barley values. But follow-up rain and a sizeable winter crop plant was likely to pressure prices.
A slightly softer international malting barley market after rain in Europe, together with rain across much of the Australian cropping area, had reassured buyers for the second half of 1997.
New crop export prices eased to about A$170.00 a tonne port. In cottonseed, rain in early May produced easing domestic demand in the latter part of the week.

However, consumption is increasing in the southern states with current crop seed now reaching feedlots and dairies in southern NSW and Victoria. Consumption by traditional northern NSW and Queensland dairies also increased.
Export activity remains high, with Japan, Korea and Taiwan continuing to discuss coverage from prompt period through until new crop 1998, concentrating on the second half of the year.
Offtake of Australian seed can be expected to maintain a steady pace throughout the season as supply from the U.S., Australia's major comeptitor, will be limited.
Australian seed may come under limited competition from Argentina and Africa, but should remain favoured supplier.
Seed prices have maintained their recent strength, trading up to A$150.00 a tonne Darling Downs gin. Central Queensland seed continues to trade at about A$145.00 a tonne ex gin.
New crop pulses market looks promising for chickpeas and faba beans as old crop prices firm and much of old crop carryout stock is shipped on a heavy schedule from southern ports.
Demand from the Indian subcontinent had increased markedly in recent months on the prospect of lower production this year.
While the short-term Middle Eastern market was reasonably well covered for faba beans, strength in related pulses should see the market relatively stable over the coming season.
Recent market movements point to chickpea prices around A$300.00 a tonne delivered port and faba beans at about A$250.00 a tonne port for the new crop.
Favourable crush margins for sunflower seed have produced increased demand despite a recent price fall in sunflower oil.

Domestic values rose over the past week, with sunflowers finishing at A$320.00 a tonne delivered Darling Downs and A$332.00 a tonne delivered Newcastle for May. Central Queensland sunflower prices finished around A$277.00-A$282.00 depot for May-July. New crop soybean prices also traded higher at A$430.00 a tonne Brisbane.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
